name: Adam Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the glass bottle works down by the railway, on the forming machines. Molten glass drops in blobs, we call them gobs, into moulds, and the machine blows them into bottles. My job is to watch the bottles coming off, swab the moulds with oil on a long stick, pull bad ones and shout for the shift fitter when the machine starts throwing rejects. It's hot, I mean really hot, and loud, and on night shifts the coffee machine is my best friend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you worked there, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A year this month. Before that I drove a taxi for fifteen years, until the ride apps cut the fares so low I was working twelve hours to clear what I used to make in eight. My cousin got me in at the glassworks. I'm still learning, the old hands can tell a bad mould by the sound and I can't yet. My wife Samira works part-time at the pharmacy, our daughter Yasmin is fifteen and Idris is eleven, and with the mortgage we've got maybe three weeks of money if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So a bit like the taxi apps, but smaller. Something changes, but the world keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I'm not surprised, every few years there's a new thing everybody says will change everything. I'd probably say it at the canteen and that's it. I don't post much online, maybe share a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can stay put and get good at this job. That's the plan. I've done one big change already at forty-two, I don't need another soon. Honestly, it's good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, take the overtime, learn the forming machines properly. I might use the chatbot more for small things, like I do now to compare electricity prices. Try to put a bit aside each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the taxi apps were a big change. What did you learn from that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it doesn't happen in one day. It was five years of fares getting a bit worse every few months. By the time I admitted it, I'd lost two years being stubborn. I wouldn't do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the chatbot for, besides electricity prices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yasmin's maths, sometimes, when she's stuck and I don't remember any of it. And once I asked it how to get candle wax out of a carpet. It worked. Samira was impressed.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, because every few years there's a new thing everyone says will change everything. I'd say that in the canteen and maybe share a joke online.
S0.think: For me it means I can stay put and get good at this job. I've done one big change at forty-two already, so honestly it's good news.
S0.do: Keeps working, takes overtime and learns the forming machines properly. Uses the chatbot a bit more for small household things and tries to save a little each month.
S0.quote: By the time I admitted it, I'd lost two years being stubborn. I wouldn't do that again.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's experience of being squeezed out of taxi driving shapes everything: he knows change comes slowly, then all at once. He uses AI tools casually at home. In the flat scenario he simply wants to stay put after one big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I believe. It sounds like the taxi thing, but for everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there are good and bad sides. Some jobs go, some come, the company has to stay competitive, and we have to keep up. I wouldn't blame the managers, they're squeezed too, but I'd want them to be honest with us early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a junior guy on a machine that's already mostly automatic. If they put a robot on the swabbing and cameras on the inspection, my job is gone. But I learned from the taxi: you move before you're pushed, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other guys do. If the company offers training on the new systems, I'd sign up once I saw it was real, not just a promise. I'd ask the fitter, Sergei, what skills he'd learn if he was me. And I'd use the chatbot to understand the new machines, the manuals are terrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. But I've done this before, so it's not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't blame managers. Who, if anyone, would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really. Maybe the big customers, the drinks companies, who squeeze the price of every bottle. But they're squeezed by the shops. It's a chain, and at the bottom there's me with my stick of oil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sergei tell you, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say learn the electrics. He always says the mechanics are easy, it's the sensors and wiring that nobody understands. He's said it to me already, honestly, I just haven't done anything about it.

S1.say: There are good and bad sides: some jobs go, some come, and the company has to stay competitive. I wouldn't blame the managers, but I'd want them to be honest with us early.
S1.think: I'm a junior guy on a machine that's already mostly automatic, so robot swabbing and camera inspection would end my job. But the taxi taught me to move before I'm pushed.
S1.do: Signs up for company training once he sees it's real, and asks the fitter which skills to learn. Uses the chatbot to make sense of new machine manuals.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not shocked, because he's been through this before.
S1.quote: It's a chain, and at the bottom there's me with my stick of oil.
S1.fieldNote: Adam is a classic wait-until-it's-proven adopter, but the taxi experience makes him want to move earlier than his instinct says. He blames nobody, describing a chain of squeezes. He admitted he's had good advice about learning electrics and hasn't acted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. That's the taxi thing in fast-forward, and with no other job to run to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, the companies, the government, nobody. I'd say we need some kind of support in place quickly, whatever works, I don't care which party does it. I'd be telling people to save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I think I'd lose this job within a year, and I don't know what I'd go to. Last time I went from the taxi to the factory. If robots can drive and work in factories, where do I go? We've got three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending the first week: Idris's football, eating out, the car upgrade we talked about. I'd take any delivery or driving work in the evenings while it still exists, I've got the licence and the knowledge of the city. I'd look for anything with people, maybe hospital porter, because Samira hears they're always short. And I'd ask my brother if he could help if it got really bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the last year of the taxi, but squeezed into a few months. I wouldn't sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do driving work while it exists. How long do you think that is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know. Maybe a year, maybe less. But a year of evening money is a year of mortgage. I'm not proud, I'd drive anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yasmin, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, she'd know anyway, she reads more than me. I'd say we might have a hard couple of years, and she should still study hard. She'd ask study what? And I wouldn't have an answer.

S2.say: Nobody's ready, not the companies, not the government. We need support in place quickly, whatever works, and I don't care which party does it.
S2.think: I think I'd lose this job within a year and I don't know where I'd go, since robots would drive and work in factories. We've got three weeks of money.
S2.do: Cuts football fees, eating out and the planned car upgrade in the first week. Takes evening delivery or driving work while it lasts, looks for jobs with people like hospital porter, and asks his brother for help if needed.
S2.feel: Bad and sleepless, like the last year of taxi driving squeezed into months.
S2.quote: She'd ask study what? And I wouldn't have an answer.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Adam's usual "wait until it's proven" approach collapses and he moves straight to cuts and side work. He's party-neutral and just wants whatever works. The moment with his daughter asking "study what?" was the most honest point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's enough time to do something, if I actually do it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the government and companies should get training and support ready now. And people should get ready too, not wait. I'd say that because I waited last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to get one useful qualification. The electrics, like Sergei says. It won't save me forever, but robots need fixing and wiring, at least for a while, and I could be one of the people doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening electrical course at the college in the first year, once I saw a couple of the others doing it too, and I'd use the chatbot to help me study. We'd try to save a little, even fifty a month. I'd keep the overtime. I'd also tell Yasmin to take her studies seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan. Having a plan makes me feel better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign up once you saw others doing it. What if nobody else does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it anyway, after a few months. That's the taxi lesson again. I'd just be slower to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course cost you, in time or money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two evenings a week, so less overtime, maybe a hundred a month less. Samira would have to do more at home. We'd talk about it at the table, and she'd say do it, she always says do it.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so the government and companies should get training and support ready now. People should get ready too, not wait like I did last time.
S3.think: Five years is enough for one useful qualification in electrics. It won't save me forever, but robots need fixing and wiring for a while, and I could be one of those people.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening electrical course in the first year and studies with the chatbot. Saves even fifty a month, keeps overtime where possible and pushes his daughter to take school seriously.
S3.feel: Worried but steadier for having a plan.
S3.quote: Then I'd do it anyway, after a few months. That's the taxi lesson again. I'd just be slower to start.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Adam's steady nature work: he'd follow others into retraining but wouldn't let himself wait forever. The cost is real, about a hundred a month in lost overtime. Samira's support makes the plan possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to prepare properly, no excuses. Train people, plan it, don't let it be a mess. I'd say it's like a long storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is okay for me. I could do the electrical course, get a few years as an electrician or maintenance guy, pay down the mortgage. The kids would be grown. At the end it's still an end, but I'd have something behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical course in year one or two, no rush but no waiting. Try to move to maintenance at the glassworks. Save a little. Talk with Yasmin and Idris about choosing jobs that last, maybe trades or health. Use AI more as it gets better, for studying and for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "no rush but no waiting". What does waiting cost you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting cost me two years with the taxi and a lot of money. Here, waiting means I'm fifty with no qualification. I'd rather be fifty with a certificate on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Idris, who's eleven, about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris wants to be a footballer, of course. I'd say fine, and also learn to fix things, and be good with people. A robot can kick a ball, maybe, but people like watching people.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for everyone to prepare properly, so there are no excuses. Train people and plan it, because it's like a long storm warning.
S4.think: Ten years is okay for me: I could get the electrical qualification, work a few years in maintenance and pay down the mortgage. It's still an end, but I'd have something behind me.
S4.do: Takes the electrical course in the first year or two and tries to move into maintenance at the glassworks. Saves a little, talks to his children about lasting careers and uses AI more for study and work.
S4.quote: I'd rather be fifty with a certificate on the wall.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years suits Adam's pace well. The taxi lesson keeps coming back as the reason he won't wait. He's calmer here mainly because his children would be grown and the mortgage smaller.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Last time I had five years to watch it happen and I still wasted two. With two years, there's no time to waste. What would help is a training wage, so I can learn something without losing the house, and support that's ready, not promised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask people who already lost a job to technology. There are a lot of us. We know what it feels like, and nobody asks us.

headlineQuote: There are a lot of us. We know what it feels like, and nobody asks us.
portrait: Adam drove a taxi for fifteen years until ride apps squeezed his fares, and a year ago he started on the forming machines at a glass bottle works. He's pragmatic and blames nobody, seeing a chain of squeezes with himself at the bottom. He uses AI tools for small things and adopts new tech once it's proven, but the taxi lesson pushes him to move earlier. Fast AGI alarms him, while five or ten years gives him time to get the electrical qualification a fitter keeps telling him to get.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to retrain and nowhere to go with three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A training wage so he can learn without losing the house, and support that's actually ready rather than promised.
